statement: In Pre-Norm transformers the learnable scale vector of a normalization layer does not increase expressivity, but it improves optimization through a self-amplifying preconditioning effect on the following linear map; removing scale vectors substantially degrades pre-training despite their negligible parameter count.

scope.model: Pre-Norm decoder-only large language models with learnable-scale normalization layers
scope.budget: language-model pre-training; the cited work does not state a fixed wall-clock budget

locators.location: abstract, arXiv 2605.26895v1, retrieved verbatim from the arXiv Atom API
locators.excerpt: we show empirically that although scale vectors constitute only a negligible fraction of model parameters, removing them substantially degrades LLM pre-training. Our theory further shows that, in Pre-Norm architectures, scale vectors do not increase expressivity; instead, they improve optimization through a self-amplifying preconditioning effect on subsequent linear mappings.

metrics.name: pretraining_loss_when_scale_vectors_removed
metrics.result: Reported as substantial degradation; the abstract gives no effect size. The campaign's baseline calls F.rms_norm(x, (x.size(-1),)) with NO learnable weight, so it sits on the degraded side of this ablation by construction.

assessment.rationale: This is the most directly actionable literature finding for the active baseline, because the baseline lacks the component entirely rather than mis-tuning it: train.py's norm() is a bare F.rms_norm with no learnable scale, and the architecture is Pre-Norm (x = x + attn(norm(x))), which is exactly the regime the claim addresses. Directness is direct -- the paper ablates the scale vector itself. Scope match is only PARTIAL and the gap is the important part: the cited work studies large models without a stated wall-clock constraint, while this campaign runs 50.33M parameters under 300 charged seconds. Adding scale vectors adds parameters and a small amount of per-step work, so under a fixed-time budget it must pay for the steps it costs -- an optimization benefit demonstrated at scale and at unbounded horizon does not automatically survive that trade. The abstract also reports no effect size, so nothing here predicts a magnitude against our 0.000426 gate. Risk of bias medium: abstract only, single group, no artifact examined. Treat as a well-motivated mechanism to test, not as a result to assume.
